query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Incrementally increasing the Ti content in CoCrFeMnNi-based HEA protective coatings enhances wear resistance by increasing lattice distortion and impeding dislocation mobility up to an optimal Ti concentration, after which further increases lead to deleterious phase changes or microstructural coarsening that degrade wear performance.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy coating with baseline (minimal) Ti content.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the Ti content (e.g., x = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, and 1 in CoCrFeMnNiTix coatings).
generation.conditions: Dry sliding wear tests at room temperature under controlled load and sliding speed, with coatings prepared via magnetron sputtering.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion and dislocation mobility in the coating microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Ti addition increases lattice distortion which hinders dislocation glide during deformation. This modified dislocation mobility changes the balance between work hardening and softening mechanisms, leading to improved resistance against abrasive and adhesive wear until excessive Ti causes phase segregation or coarser microstructural features that reduce wear performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: An initial decrease in friction coefficient and lower wear loss at moderate Ti additions (e.g., around Ti0.5–Ti0.75), followed by an increase in wear indicators at higher Ti levels.
generation.baseline: Coating performance of a CoCrFeMnNi HEA with minimal or no Ti addition.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for magnetron sputtered HEA coatings under typical dry sliding conditions at room temperature; effects may differ under varying temperatures or loading conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal Ti concentration and the magnitude of changes in wear performance are uncertain due to potential complex interactions such as phase formation and microstructural evolution that may vary with processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CoCrFeMnNiTix coatings with systematically increasing Ti content using identical processing parameters. Conduct standardized dry sliding wear tests at room temperature, while concurrently characterizing microstructural features (e.g., lattice distortion and dislocation structures) using TEM and SEM.
measurements: Friction coefficient and wear rate from wear tests
Microstructural analysis to quantify lattice distortion and dislocation density
Phase identification using XRD to detect any phase segregation at high Ti contents
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental data do not show an initial improvement (i.e., reduced wear loss and friction coefficient) with moderate Ti addition linked to increased lattice distortion and reduced dislocation mobility, or if increased Ti continuously improves or has no measurable effect on wear performance, then the mechanistic hypothesis is falsified.

Therefore, it indicated that the specimens’ deformation was only controlled by the dislocation slip. Further magnified TEM images revealed more dense and complex dislocation structures. A large number of dislocation fragments and loops filled the entire image, making it difficult to distinguish individual dislocation structures. The high dislocation density and the existence of a dislocation network also confirmed the high plasticity of the alloy at 673 K. Figure 9 shows the true stress–strain curves of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA at different deformation strain rates and temperatures. It was found that all curves had similar trends. That is, with the rise of the strain, the flow stress increased to the peak stress first and then decreased as the strain continued to increase. Before it reached the peak stress, the flow stress rose along with the strain. At this stage, the dislocation density increased due to deformation, the dislocation accumulation increased the deformation resistance, and a work hardening was the main rheological feature. When the flow stress achieved its maximal stress, it steadily declined as the strain increased. This is attributed to the dynamic recovery or dynamic recrystallization softening mechanism in the material exceeding the work-hardening mechanism, which is macrographically manifested as a gradual reduction in the flow stress []. In fact, the process of thermal deformation of materials is a competitive process of work-hardening and softening mechanisms, and the effects of hardening and softening reach an equilibrium when the flow stress reaches the peak stress []. The analysis of the coatings was performed via grazing incidence at a low angle of 1°, in order to exclude the crystalline structure of the substrate. The coating hardness values exhibited approximately threefold greater values compared to the substrate hardness values across all cladding conditions. Microhardness values of 540 ± 10 HV0.1 were obtained at an ultrasonic amplitude of 5 µm, which was higher than the values of 505 ± 10 HV0.1, 490 ± 10 HV0.1, and 460 ± 10 HV0.1 recorded with amplitudes of 15 µm, WOU, and WU of 10 µm, respectively. The increased microhardness at 5 µm is attributed to ultrasonic vibrations’ acoustic and cavitation effects. The friction coefficient was found to be stable and at its lowest when using an ultrasonic amplitude of 5 µm, compared to greater amplitudes of WOU and WU. The 3D surface profile of the wear reveals that ultrasonic assistance at a 5 µm amplitude results in a lower scar depth. This indicates that the coating generated with the assistance of ultrasonic vibrations has excellent antifriction capabilities, and the wear mechanism was dominated by abrasive and oxidative wear with fewer grooves and debris.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.3. High Temperature Friction and Wear Properties of HEA Coatings
cited_evidence.text: The worn surfaces microstructure of the AlCoCrFeNi and AlCoCrFeNiW0.5 coatings at 800 °Care presented in Figure 8a,b. The discontinuous distribution of the adhesive layer represents the occurrence of adhesive wear during the wear process. Obvious plastic deformation occurred on both surfaces of AlCoCrFeNi and AlCoCrFeNiW0.5 coatings. Strong resistance of high temperature softening induced by dynamic recrystallization (involving dislocation tangles, and formation of dislocation cell structures and sub-grains) in the BCC HEA was reported recently, which indicates that dislocation tangles, and formation of dislocation cell structures and sub-grains play an importance role in the high temperature mechanical properties []. According to Orowan’s strengthening mechanism, lattice distortion can increase lattice stress. Lattice distortion of BCC phase for AlCoCrFeNiW0.5 HEA coating also plays a contributory role. Therefore, the BCC phase in the AlCoCrFeNiW0.5 coating has better resistance to damage under the same external forces at high temperatures. Moreover, the W-rich hard phases also contribute to improving the plastic deformation resistance of the matrix.

In the case of dry sliding, a pin-disc friction and wear testing machine (HT-600, Zhongke KaiHua Co., Ltd., Lanzhou, China) was employed to conduct wear experiments on the coating. The speed was set at 500 r/min, the test force was 40 N, the test time was 1200 s, and the test torque was 1.366 N·m. Wear samples were prepared in the form of disks with a diameter of approximately 25 mm and a thickness of approximately 10 mm. Si3N4 pellets with a hardness of 75 HRC and a diameter of 50 HRC were employed as the dual samples. The wear surface morphology and wear mechanism were examined using SEM and a three-dimensional noncontact morphometer (PS50, NANOVEA, Irvine, CA, USA).

With the increase in Ti content, the friction coefficient and wear loss decreased first and then increased. The lowest values of the Ti0.75 coating were 0.296 and 0.001 g. When the x value reached 0.25 (Ti0.25), the coating’s adhesion and abrasive wear mechanisms remained unchanged, the coating surface’s adhesion degree decreased visibly, and the wear resistance was effectively enhanced. The wear marks of the CoCrFeMnNiTix (x = 0.5, 0.75, and 1) high-entropy alloy coatings showed visible stratification and lamellar morphology. With the increase in Ti content, the coating’s wear mechanism changed from adhesive wear and abrasive wear to fatigue wear and abrasive wear.

To evaluate the mechanical performance of HEA, hardness was evaluated with loading of 5 N and a corresponding holding time of 15 s. Each Vickers hardness value was obtained by averaging 10 indents tests on a mirror-like surface. To explore the wear resistance of HEA, the tribological behavior of HEA sliding under dry conditions and lubrication was evaluated by using a ball-on-disk tribometer (HT-1000), selecting Al2O3 balls as the grinding material. The test was carried out at a normal load of 10 N with a sliding speed of 0.18 m s−1 and a duration of 30 min. Each wear test was repeated at least three times to ensure reliability. The friction coefficient was recorded in real time by software. The density of samples was measured by Archimedes’ drainage method (ZMD-2). The weight loss was derived from the quality difference of the patterns before and after the friction test, and each mass was weighed more than five times to reduce the error.

reading.lever: Vary Ti content incrementally in HEA coatings to modulate lattice distortion and dislocation mobility.
reading.why: Because related studies on CoCrFeMnNiTix coatings showed that controlled Ti adjustment shifts wear mechanism and adhesion, offering a direct handle to test the mechanistic hypothesis in high-entropy protective coatings.
